title: Distinguish borrowed streams from factory-acquired resources
applies_when: A Python stream/archive wrapper adds cleanup on failure or explicit close. Determine whether the caller supplied an existing handle or the API acquired the resource; do not test only the owning factory path.
lesson: Inspect the owning caller before adding cleanup to the wrapper. In pinned AnyIO, TLSStream.wrap receives an existing transport; a failed wrapper does not make the original caller handle inaccessible. connect_tcp and TLSConnectable acquire transports and forcefully close them on BaseException. TLSListener delegates failed or cancelled handshakes to a handler whose documented first action is forceful close. Test real protocol failure and cancellation after ClientHello, observe peer EOF and actual handle closure, and retain a direct-wrap control where the caller closes its borrowed transport. For archive close fixes, pair immediate cached-publication tests with caller-owned BytesIO and file controls, keeping the wrapper alive after close. Fsspec PR2313's generic __exit__ call closes both borrowed handles early; PR2312 restricts cleanup to OpenFile. Idempotency does not establish ownership. An encrypted send losing a TLS record is a different state-integrity contract; its broken flag is not proof of handshake ownership transfer.
avoid_when: An API may explicitly transfer ownership even on failure; inspect its documented contract and actual callers. A new supported owning path, source drift, a distinct cancellation phase, external SSLContext implementation or platform can invalidate this example. Do not universally waive cleanup of failed acquisitions, add unconditional close of caller-owned resources, or infer permanent leakage from a retained handle alone. Native Windows CPython3.12 loopback controls do not qualify every SSL implementation or platform. This lesson supplies a next check, not an automatic no-bug verdict, measured selector gain or PR-yield claim.

evidence.note: wrap accepts the caller's existing transport and performs the handshake. This source does not by itself promise failure-time ownership transfer or establish a production leak.
TLSListener documents forceful close and invokes the error handler on BaseException from the handshake. This is owning-caller cleanup omitted by the wrap-only window.
TLSConnectable closes its acquired stream on BaseException before propagating the error. Source mechanism, not an exhaustive runtime guarantee.
connect_tcp independently closes a newly connected transport when TLS wrapping fails.

The truststore certificate-failure test keeps the original TCP stream in async-with around wrap, illustrating explicit caller ownership. Optional truststore behavior is not every SSLContext implementation.

PR2313 calls __exit__ on any supplied context after ZIP close and clears of. Cached-publication regressions pass, but native Windows public BytesIO/file controls both fail because close now closes the caller's handle. CI success did not cover this contract.

Existing author PR2312 includes caller-owned buffer/file, owned OpenFile, cached publication, open-member retry and upload-error cases. Native Windows caller controls and its 49-test ZIP suite pass at this head. This is independent validation, not our PR or a full CI/Linux qualification.
